source.title: Challenge: Hand coding weights for efficient sequence memorisation

record.file_problem: The supplied post is readable in full, but formatting has removed some numbers and mathematical expressions, including parts of figure captions and reported comparisons.
record.tranche_reason: It applies gradient-based training to random-label sequence memorization in toy transformer and MLP architectures and reports classification accuracy and capacity. This extends the claim to a new task and model setting.
record.gate_note: The post reports its own trained-model capacity and accuracy results. The cited results from other work and the commenters' experiments are not rows. Several fitted comparisons and figure values are missing from the supplied text because of formatting loss.
record.test_reason: The study measures random sequence memorization capacity in shallow transformer and MLP models. V1 specifies convolutional networks on CIFAR-10/100; none of the other versions names the experiments performed here. Architectural capacity comparisons alone do not test depth degradation, initialization effects, learning-rate stability, or batch-normalization training speed.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate but omits the central construction challenge and hybrid result. The authors find approximately parameter-count scaling of trained sequence memorization capacity. Their hand-coded construction approximately matches the trained scaling exponent at 90% accuracy with roughly 9.7 times fewer facts, falls further behind at 100%, and improves when its unembedding is trained. They report an unexplained architectural outlier and caution against overinterpreting fitted exponents.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses toy sequence memorization with random labels and one-layer transformer/MLP variants, rather than the CIFAR image-classification settings in V1. Trained runs use Adam; the architecture sweep uses up to 50,000 epochs with learning-rate reductions when needed.
record.method_sensitivity: Architecture settings change capacity; the MLP has the largest reported effect, while the MLP-plus-norms/no-residual/no-bias/ReLU combination performs unusually poorly. Learned attention is less stable than the other mixing variants.

fits_no_version.finding: Adam-trained shallow sequence models memorize random mappings perfectly at selected dataset sizes; maximum memorized facts grows with model size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient training can achieve perfect random sequence memorization in shallow transformer and MLP models, with capacity increasing with model size.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding an MLP increases maximum memorized facts by 60%–373% in the reported comparisons; one norms/no-residual/no-bias/ReLU configuration performs unusually poorly.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture choices affect attainable random sequence memorization capacity under the tested Adam recipe.

fits_no_version.finding: Trained, hybrid, and hand-coded models differ in capacity prefactors and scaling at the 90% and 100% accuracy thresholds.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The tested hand-coded construction stores fewer random sequence facts than fully trained models; training its unembedding improves capacity.

record.problems: The task and architectures differ from CIFAR convolutional classification. Numerical values are missing from several fitted comparisons and figures in the supplied text. The authors note that some architecture effects may reflect trainability rather than representational capacity, and report an unexplained outlier configuration. Fitted exponents are explicitly cautioned against being taken too seriously.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows extracted. The supplied text references figures and tables with numerical values that are absent or garbled; those values cannot be assigned to specific models or settings.

untested.parts: Training error of sufficiently large CIFAR-10/100 convolutional networks, including random labels, and the stated smaller-model, stopping, and regularization conditions.
Teacher-student ReLU problems, spurious local minima, and the effect of one or two extra student neurons.
Training degradation with increasing depth and its prevention by identity shortcuts or special initialization.
Activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation, training speed, and trainable depth.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, loss transients, curvature, and edge-of-stability dynamics.
Batch normalization's effects on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons. The study uses RMSNorm and measures capacity.

record.verdict_notes: The 100% success criterion is used to select maximum dataset sizes; it does not imply reliable success across initializations. Main plots and architecture comparisons emphasize success in any of 11 runs. Commenters' experiments are separate contributions and are not treated as this study's results.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 convolutional networks, Adam/SGD comparisons, early stopping and regularized recipes as claim conditions; results are for toy sequence models and random input-to-label mappings.

rows.subject: trained toy model (architecture sweep; aggregate)
rows.size_stated: All models used the same size; values missing in supplied text.
rows.operation_detail: Trained each architectural variant with gradient descent (Adam) on cross-entropy loss; maximum learnable facts found by binary search.

conditions.value: All combinations of mixing, MLP, norms, residual, bias, and activation variants

rows.baseline: Architecture variants compared pairwise; exact values are in referenced Appendix B tables, whose numerical contents are not present in the supplied text.
rows.value: Adding an MLP block lets networks learn 60%–373% more facts.
rows.uncertainty: 11 differently initialized runs per tested fact count; four repeated binary searches; main analysis uses the 'Any' criterion.
rows.note: Aggregate effect across settings; the post says the MLP has the largest effect.
rows.check: This measures the increase in maximum memorized facts from adding an MLP, not any specified version. The reported 60%–373% comparison excludes the outlier configuration and uses the best-of-11 success criterion.

rows.subject: trained toy model (architecture outlier; aggregate across mixing variants)
rows.size_stated: Same single model size as architecture sweep; exact values missing.
rows.operation_detail: Trained an MLP configuration with norms, no residual around the MLP, no bias, and ReLU activation.

conditions.value: learned attention, uniform attention, or dual embedding

rows.baseline: Removing the MLP; exact value not stated.
rows.value: Did really badly, almost as badly as (and in one case slightly worse than) removing the MLP.
rows.locator: Results; Appendix B, 'MLP + Norms + No Residual around MLP + No Bias + ReLU'
rows.note: This is a stated training failure for a configuration, although the authors say they do not know whether it reflects training dynamics or architectural limits.
rows.check: Lower maximum memorization capacity does not establish absent training success: the models still learn all facts at their measured capacity. The authors leave architectural capacity versus optimization unresolved. Neither depth nor batch normalization is tested.

rows.subject: fully trained toy models
rows.size_stated: Model dimension varied; exact values missing in supplied text.
rows.operation_detail: Fit scaling line to trained-model maximum-fact results at two accuracy thresholds.
rows.measure: Fitted scaling exponent and capacity comparison.
rows.value: Trained model fitted exponent 1.97; hand-coded models have a worse prefactor, described elsewhere as roughly 9.7× fewer facts at 90% accuracy.
rows.uncertainty: The authors caution that fitted exponents should not be taken too seriously; exact fit uncertainty not stated.
rows.note: The post also says the 90%-accuracy hand-coded model matches trained scaling behaviour, but with a lower prefactor.
rows.check: The fitted capacity exponent at a selected 90% accuracy threshold does not measure near-zero training error in CIFAR convolutional networks. The threshold permits 10% error.

rows.subject: fully trained toy models
rows.size_stated: Model dimension varied; exact values missing in supplied text.
rows.operation_detail: Fit scaling line to trained-model maximum-fact results at 100% accuracy.
rows.measure: Fitted scaling exponent and capacity comparison.
rows.baseline: Fully hand-coded model; exact fitted exponent and comparison values are missing from the supplied text.
rows.value: Trained-model fitted exponent 2.04; the text says hand-coded models fall further behind as models grow, reaching about 27× fewer facts at a model size whose value is missing, with the gap widening.
rows.uncertainty: The authors caution that fitted exponents should not be taken too seriously; exact fit uncertainty not stated.
rows.note: The reported 100% accuracy criterion measures exact classification of the facts in this task.
rows.check: Perfect memorization is demonstrated for selected dataset sizes in a shallow sequence model, outside V1's specified systems and datasets. The capacity exponent and hand-coded comparison do not establish V1.

rows.subject: hybrid toy models (hand-coded embeddings, trained unembedding)
rows.size_stated: Model dimension varied; exact values missing in supplied text.
rows.stage_stated: unembedding trained with Adam; embeddings hand-coded
rows.operation_detail: Train only the unembedding while using the hand-coded embedding construction.
rows.measure: Fitted scaling exponents and maximum facts learned.
rows.baseline: Fully trained fitted exponents 1.97 (at least 90%) and 2.04 (100%).
rows.value: Hybrid fitted exponents 2.04 (at least 90%) and 2.09 (100%); it significantly outperforms the hand-coded model, but the stated numerical capacity factors are absent or differ across sections.
rows.uncertainty: The authors caution that fitted exponents should not be taken too seriously; exact fit uncertainty not stated.
rows.note: Comparator row: the hybrid model is not fully gradient-trained from random initialization.
rows.check: The hybrid uses hand-coded embeddings and trains only the unembedding. Its capacity scaling does not test random-initialization training of the networks named in V1 or an initialization-speed comparison under V4.
